label: main
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: cor:numerical-solvability
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:numerical-solvability}
Assume the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{main}.
The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item There is a K\"ahler class $\kappa$ such that, for every irreducible
analytic subvariety $Y\subset X$ of dimension $k$, including $Y=X$, and
every $n-d\le q\le\min\{k,n-1\}$,
\begin{equation}\label{mixed-numerical}
 \int_Y\kappa^{k-q}\wedge\bigl(\Lambda\wedge e^\alpha\bigr)^{[q]}>0 .
\end{equation}
\item There is a smooth
$\underline\omega\in \alpha$ with
$A_{\underline\omega}(x)\in\mathcal A$ for every $x\in X$.
\item Equation~\eqref{target} has a smooth admissible solution in
$\alpha$.
\end{enumerate}
 When these conditions
hold, there is $\delta_{\mathrm{num}}>0$ such that, for every K\"ahler class
$\kappa$,
\begin{equation}\label{uniform-numerical}
 \int_Y\kappa^{k-q}\wedge\bigl(\Lambda\wedge e^\alpha\bigr)^{[q]}
 \ge\delta_{\mathrm{num}}\int_Y\kappa^{k-q}\wedge [\chi]^q
\end{equation}
for all $Y$ and $q$ as in \textup{(i)}.
head: environment

label: mainNHR
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{mainNHR}
Let $\alpha=[\omega_0]\in H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)$. 
Suppose that either
\begin{itemize}
\item 
$\Lambda$ determines a spectral equation satisfying the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{main} and one of the equivalent conditions in Corollary~\ref{cor:numerical-solvability} holds; or
\item there exists $\omega\in \alpha$ that solves \eqref{general-equation} and satisfies
\ref{H1}--\ref{H2} of Section~\ref{nhr:section}.
\end{itemize}
Then the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item\label{mainNHR-a}
For K\"ahler classes $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_j$,
$0\le j\le d-2$, the pairing
\begin{equation}\label{intro-NHR}
(\gamma,\eta)\longmapsto
\int_X\gamma\eta\,\beta_1\cdots\beta_j
\bigl(\Lambda\wedge e^\alpha\bigr)^{[n-j-2]}
\end{equation}
has signature $(1,h^{1,1}(X)-1)$ and is negative
definite on
\[
\left\{\gamma\in H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R):
\int_X\gamma\,\beta_1\cdots\beta_j
\bigl(\Lambda\wedge e^\alpha\bigr)^{[n-j-1]}=0
\right\}.
\]
For $j=0$, the product of the $\beta_i$ is $1$.
\item\label{mainNHR-b}
There exists $\varepsilon_0>0$ such that for every $N\ge1$, nef classes
$\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_N$, and
$0\le\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0$, the degree-$d$
homogeneous polynomial in $(y,\mathbf{x})$, where $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$,
\begin{equation}\label{intro-master}
\mathcal T_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(y,\mathbf{x})
=y^d\left[\mathcal I\!\left(\alpha+
\frac1y\sum_{i=1}^N x_i\beta_i\right)
+\varepsilon \right]
\end{equation}
is a Lorentzian polynomial.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: def:garding-ideal
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:garding-ideal}
For a real nonzero polynomial $G$ in $n$ variables, its \emph{G\aa rding component}
is the connected component $\mathcal C_G$ of $\{G>0\}$ satisfying
\[
 \mathcal C_G+\mathbb R^n_{>0}\subset\mathcal C_G,
\]
when such a component exists. Here $\mathbb R^n_{>0}=\{(x_1,\cdots,x_n)|\,x_i>0\}$.

All nonnegative constant polynomials, including the zero polynomial,
are G\aa rding and ideal G\aa rding. By convention their G\aa rding
components are $\mathbb R^n$; in particular, $\mathcal C_0=\mathbb R^n$.
For nonconstant polynomials, define recursively:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $G$ is \emph{G\aa rding} if $\mathcal C_G$ exists, every 
partial derivative $\partial_iG$ is G\aa rding, and
\[
 \mathcal C_G\subset
 \bigcap_{i}\mathcal C_{\partial_iG}.
\]
\item $G$ is \emph{ideal G\aa rding} if it is G\aa rding,
$\mathcal C_G$ is convex, and every partial derivative
$\partial_iG$ is ideal G\aa rding.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: G\aa rding and ideal G\aa rding polynomials

label: polarization
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: idealinputs
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{idealinputs}
Let $G$ be a nonzero ideal G\aa rding polynomial.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item Its G\aa rding component is convex and invariant under
nonnegative coordinate translations. Every nonzero iterated derivative
in nonnegative directions is ideal G\aa rding and is positive on $\mathcal C_G$;
its G\aa rding component contains $\mathcal C_G$.
\item If $F$ is such a derivative (including $G$ itself) of degree $m\ge1$, then $F^{1/m}$
and $\log F$ are concave on $\mathcal C_F$.
\item If $v\ge0$ and $\partial_vG\not\equiv0$, then $G/\partial_vG$ is concave on
$\mathcal C_{\partial_vG}$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: def:ige
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:ige}
Nonnegative constants, including zero, are G\aa rding elliptic and
ideal, with component $\mathcal Q(E)$.
A nonconstant real polynomial $G$ on $\mathcal Q(E)$ is a
\emph{G\aa rding elliptic operator} if it has a component $\mathcal C_G$ of
$\{G>0\}$ satisfying
\[
 \mathcal C_G+\mathcal Q(E)^+\subset\mathcal C_G,
\]
and every nonzero derivative $\partial_DG$, $D\ge0$, is G\aa rding
elliptic with $\mathcal C_G\subset\mathcal C_{\partial_DG}$.
We call $\mathcal C_G$ its \emph{G\aa rding component}.

Such an operator is \emph{ideal} if the G\aa rding components of all
its nonzero iterated derivatives in semipositive directions are convex,
including $G$ itself.
head: environment
name: G\aa rding and ideal G\aa rding elliptic operators

label: ige:basic
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{ige:basic}
Let $G$ be a G\aa rding elliptic operator on $\mathcal Q(E)$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item For $A\in\mathcal C_G$ and $D_1,\ldots,D_N\ge0$ with $\sum_iD_i>0$, the
\emph{positive scalarization}
\[
 f(\mathbf{x})=G\left(A+\sum_ix_iD_i\right),\qquad \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb R^N,
\]
is G\aa rding, with component
\[
 \mathcal C_f=\left\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb R^N:A+\sum_ix_iD_i\in\mathcal C_G\right\}.
\]
\item $G$ is ideal if and only if all its positive scalarizations are ideal
G\aa rding polynomials.
\item If $G$ is ideal and $F=\partial_{P_1}\cdots\partial_{P_k}G\not\equiv0$,
where $P_i\ge0$ and $k\ge0$, then $F$ is ideal G\aa rding elliptic with
$\mathcal C_G\subset\mathcal C_F$. For $m=\deg F\ge1$, both $F^{1/m}$ and $\log F$
are concave on $\mathcal C_F$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Part (i) is \cite[Theorem~4.7]{Linfty}.

For (ii), write $L(\mathbf{x})=A+\sum_ix_iD_i$. Directional differentiation
commutes with this affine substitution:
\[
 \partial_{x_i}(G\circ L)=(\partial_{D_i}G)\circ L.
\]
For each nonzero iterated derivative $F$ in these directions, part (i) gives
\[
 \mathcal C_{F\circ L}=L^{-1}(\mathcal C_F).
\]
If $G$ is ideal, all these inverse images are convex, so its
scalarizations are ideal. Conversely, extend the directions of any
iterated derivative $F$ to a semipositive family spanning $\mathcal Q(E)$.
Then $L$ is onto, and convexity of $\mathcal C_{F\circ L}$ implies convexity of
$\mathcal C_F=L(\mathcal C_{F\circ L})$.

For (iii), the definition shows that $F$ is ideal and
$\mathcal C_G\subset\mathcal C_F$. Apply Proposition~\ref{idealinputs} to a positive
scalarization of $F$ in a spanning family. Part (i) and an affine right
inverse of $L$ transfer the concavity inequalities to $\mathcal C_F$.
head: environment

label: ige:criterion
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{ige:criterion}
Let $G$ be a nonconstant polynomial on $\mathcal Q(E)$, and suppose
$\{G>0\}$ has a component $\mathcal C_G$ invariant under semipositive increments. If
\[
 \mathbf{x}\longmapsto G\left(A_0+\sum_ix_iD_i\right)
\]
is G\aa rding for every Hermitian $A_0$ and every semipositive family
with $\sum_iD_i>0$, then $G$ is G\aa rding elliptic.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We argue by induction on the degree of $G$. If $G$ is linear, then the existence of $\mathcal C_G$ implies that $G$ is G\aa rding elliptic. 

Assume $\deg G\geq2$. Let $P,Q\ge0$ with $F=\partial_PG\not\equiv0$. Choose a semipositive
spanning family with $D_1=P$ and $D_2=Q$, and put
$L(\mathbf{x})=\sum_ix_iD_i$ and $g=G\circ L$.
 Then $L^{-1}(\mathcal C_G)$ is a connected component of $\{g>0\}$ and is invariant under nonnegative coordinate translations. Hence $\mathcal C_g=L^{-1}(\mathcal C_G)$. The inclusion $\mathcal C_g\subset\mathcal C_{\partial_{x_1}g}$ then gives
\[
 \mathcal C_g=L^{-1}(\mathcal C_G),\qquad
 \mathcal C_{\partial_{x_1}g}=L^{-1}(U),\qquad \mathcal C_G\subset U,
\]
where $U$ is the component of $\{F>0\}$ containing $\mathcal C_G$.
Since $\partial_{x_1}\partial_{x_2}g\geq0$ in $L^{-1}(U)$, $U+Q\subset U$. Since $Q$ is
arbitrary, $U$ is invariant under all semipositive increments.

Next let $A_0$ be Hermitian and $D_1',\ldots,D_M'\ge0$ with
$\sum_jD_j'>0$. 
\[\tilde{g}(y,\mathbf{x}):=G(A_0+yP+\sum_jx_jD_j')\] is G\aa rding by the assumption. Let $T>0$. For large $T$, the point $(0,T\mathbf1)$ lies in $\mathcal C_{\tilde{g}}\subset\mathcal C_{\partial_y\tilde{g}}$ and $\tilde{g} (y,\mathbf x+T\mathbf1)$ has non-negative coefficients.
\[
F\left(A_0+\sum_j(x_j+T)D_j'\right)=\partial_y\tilde{g}(0,\mathbf{x}+T\mathbf1).
\]
Since the restriction map is a weak positive linear transform with a real stable symbol, by \cite[Theorem~10.3]{Garding}, it preserves G\aa rding polynomials with nonnegative coefficients.
In particular, $\partial_y\tilde{g}(0,\mathbf{x}+T\mathbf1)$ is G\aa rding and by translation invariance, so is $\partial_y\tilde{g}(0,\mathbf{x})$. 
Induction on the degree
therefore shows that $F$ is G\aa rding elliptic with
$\mathcal C_F=U\supset\mathcal C_G$, proving the assertion.
head: environment

label: nhr:scalarization
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{nhr:scalarization}
Let $q=\sum_{j=0}^d b_j\sigma_j$ be an ideal G\aa rding polynomial on
$\mathbb R^n$, with $b_d>0$ and $1\le d\le n$.
Then $F(A)=q(\lambda(A))$ is an ideal G\aa rding
elliptic operator, with component
\[
 \mathcal C_F=\{A:\lambda(A)\in\mathcal C_q\}.
\]
For every Hermitian $A_0$ and every semipositive family
$D_1,\ldots,D_N$ with $\sum_iD_i>0$, the polynomial
\[
 f(\mathbf{x})=F\left(A_0+\sum_i x_iD_i\right),
 \qquad \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb R^N,
\]
is ideal G\aa rding and has degree $\min\{d,\operatorname{rank}D_i\}$
in each variable $x_i$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The component $\mathcal C_q$ is symmetric. Every $A\in\mathcal C_F$ can be joined by
unitary conjugation to $\operatorname{diag}\lambda(A)$, so connectedness
of $\mathcal C_q$ gives connectedness of $\mathcal C_F$. Continuity of the ordered
eigenvalues makes $\mathcal C_F$ open and closed in $\{F>0\}$, hence a connected
component. Weyl's inequalities give invariance under semipositive increments.

Fix $A_0$ and the $D_i$. Choose $a\mathbf1\in\mathcal C_q$. The translate
$g(\boldsymbol{\lambda})=q(\boldsymbol{\lambda}+a\mathbf1)$ is ideal
with nonnegative coefficients \cite[Lemma~3.1]{Ideal}. For sufficiently
large $\tau$, the matrix polynomial
\[
 M(\mathbf{x})=A_0-aI+\sum_i(x_i+\tau)D_i
\]
has positive definite constant term. Define a linear map $S$ on
multi-affine monomials by
\[
 S\left(\prod_{j\in J}\lambda_j\right)=\det M(\mathbf{x})_J,
 \qquad J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\},
\]
where $M_J$ denotes the principal submatrix indexed by $J$.
Its symbol is
\[
 S\left(\prod_{j=1}^n(\lambda_j+u_j)\right)
 =\det\left(M(\mathbf{x})+\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{u})\right).
\]
The mixed-discriminant expansion gives nonnegative coefficients.
When all $x_i,u_j$ have positive imaginary parts, the matrix has positive
definite imaginary part, so the symbol is real stable and hence ideal
G\aa rding \cite[Proposition~4.3 and Theorem~1.4(1)]{Ideal}.
The symbol criterion \cite[Theorem~10.2]{Ideal} therefore makes $Sg$
ideal G\aa rding. Since
\[
 (Sg)(\mathbf{x})
 =q\bigl(\lambda(M(\mathbf{x}))+a\mathbf1\bigr)
 =F\left(A_0+\sum_i(x_i+\tau)D_i\right),
\]
translation invariance proves the assertion about $f$.
Lemmas~\ref{ige:criterion} and \ref{ige:basic}\textup{(ii)} then show
that $F$ is ideal G\aa rding elliptic.

For the degree, put $r=\operatorname{rank}D_i$. Principal-minor expansion
gives $\deg_{x_i}f\le\min\{d,r\}$. If $r\ge d$, the coefficient of
$x_i^d$ is $b_d\sigma_d(D_i)>0$. If $r<d$, set $x_j=\tau$ for $j\ne i$.
The coefficient of $x_i^r$ is
\[
 \sigma_r(D_i)\sum_{\ell=r}^d b_\ell\,
 \sigma_{\ell-r}\left(
 \left.\left(A_0+\tau\sum_{j\ne i}D_j\right)\right|_{\ker D_i}\right),
\]
where the restriction denotes compression to $\ker D_i$.
The compression of $\sum_{j\ne i}D_j$ is positive definite there.
Thus the term $\ell=d$ has positive leading coefficient in $\tau$ of
degree $d-r$, while the other terms have smaller degree. The displayed
coefficient is therefore nonzero for large $\tau$.
head: environment

label: shiftlemma
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The diagonal polynomial $s\mapsto P_x(s\mathbf1)-b$ is negative at
$\rho_1$ and strictly increasing above it. It therefore has exactly one
root above $\rho_1$, and its positive-order derivatives retain the
monotone root sequence of \eqref{strict}. Theorem~\ref{polarization}
makes $P_x-b$ ideal G\aa rding, with first derived component $\mathcal A$.

By \eqref{componentidentity}, $P_x-b\le0$ on
$\partial\mathcal A$. Letting $b\downarrow-\delta(x)$ gives the first
inequality in \eqref{admissible-levels}. Moreover,
\[
 \overline{\mathcal C_{P_x-b}}
 \subset\overline{\mathcal A}\cap\{P_x\ge b\}.
\]
The right-hand side cannot meet $\partial\mathcal A$, where
$P_x\le-\delta(x)<b$. This proves the second assertion.
head: environment

label: rootoperator
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{rootoperator}
The spectral operator $F$ is concave and strictly elliptic on $\mathcal C_G$,
and
\[
 \operatorname{tr}(\partial F(A))\ge\left(\binom nd a_d\right)^{1/d}
 \qquad(A\in\mathcal C_G).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $G$ is ideal, Lemmas~\ref{nhr:scalarization} and
\ref{ige:basic}\textup{(iii)} give concavity of $F=G^{1/d}$ on $\mathcal C_G$.
The identity
\[
 \partial F(A)=\frac{\partial\widetilde P(A)}{dG(A)^{(d-1)/d}}
\]
gives strict ellipticity. For sufficiently large $r$, concavity gives
\[
 F(rI)\le F(A)+\partial F(A)[rI-A].
\]
Dividing by $r$ and letting $r\to\infty$ proves the trace bound.
head: environment

label: raylemma
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{raylemma}
Let $K\subset\mathcal A$ be compact and $b_0\ge0$.
There are $\varrho>0$, $L\ge1$ and $\kappa>0$, uniform for
$\underline A\in K$, $x\in X$ and $0\le b\le b_0$, such that
$\underline A-\varrho I\in\mathcal A$ and every Hermitian matrix $A$
satisfying
\[
 P_x(A)=b,\qquad A-\underline A+\varrho I\ge0
\]
obeys
\begin{equation}\label{quantitative-subsolution}
 \|A-\underline A+\varrho I\|<L.
\end{equation}
Moreover, every $A\in\mathcal A$ with $P_x(A)=b$ satisfies either
\begin{equation}\label{alternatives}
 \partial F(A)[\underline A-A]\ge\kappa\operatorname{tr}(\partial F(A)),
 \qquad\text{or}\qquad
 \partial F(A)\ge\kappa\operatorname{tr}(\partial F(A))I.
\end{equation}
The norm is induced by the trace pairing.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose $\varrho>0$ so that $U=\underline A-\varrho I$, for
$\underline A\in K$, stays in a compact subset of $\mathcal A$.
Ellipticity gives $\partial\widetilde P(U)[\zeta\zeta^*]\ge\eta>0$ uniformly for
unit vectors $\zeta$. Since $P_x$ is affine under rank-one increments,
\[
 P_x(U+r\zeta\zeta^*)-b
 =P_x(U)-b+r\,\partial\widetilde P(U)[\zeta\zeta^*].
\]
Choose $L\ge1$ so that the right-hand side is positive for
$r\ge L/\sqrt n$, uniformly for $0\le b\le b_0$.
If $N=A-U\ge0$ and $\|N\|\ge L$, an eigenvector for its largest
eigenvalue gives $N\ge(L/\sqrt n)\zeta\zeta^*$. Thus
\[
 b=P_x(U+N)\ge P_x\bigl(U+(L/\sqrt n)\zeta\zeta^*\bigr)>b,
\]
a contradiction. This proves \eqref{quantitative-subsolution}.

The alternatives are the matrix subsolution dichotomy of
Sz\'ekelyhidi \cite[Proposition~6]{Szekelyhidi}, following Guan
\cite{Guan14}. Its argument uses convexity and ellipticity of the level
sets and the boundedness just proved, so it applies to $\mathcal C_G$.
For bounded $A$, the inequalities $G(A)\ge\delta_1$ and
$G\le-\delta_1$ on $\partial\mathcal A$ place the solution matrices in
a compact subset of $\mathcal C_G$. Strict ellipticity then gives the second
alternative after decreasing $\kappa$.
head: environment

label: C0prop
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{C0prop}
Fix $T$ and let $0\leq t\leq T$. Every solution of \eqref{path} normalized by $\sup_Xv_t=0$ satisfies
\[
 \|v_t\|_{L^\infty}\le C_T.
\]
head: environment

label: tracebound
title: Proof
body_md:
Every nonzero iterated coordinate derivative of $\widetilde P$ of positive order is
positive on $\mathcal A$. Hence
\begin{align}\label{tracebound}
 0<\partial_{\mathbf1}^{d-1}\widetilde P
 &=\frac{(n-1)!}{(n-d)!}a_d\sigma_1
   +\frac{n!}{(n-d+1)!}a_{d-1},\notag\\
 \operatorname{tr}A
 &>-\frac{n a_{d-1}}{(n-d+1)a_d}
 \qquad(A\in\mathcal A).
\end{align}
Since $\underline A_t$ is bounded, this gives
\[
 \Delta_\chi v_t=\operatorname{tr}A_t-
     \operatorname{tr}\underline A_t\ge-C_T.
\]
The normalization and Green's formula then yield
$\int_X(-v_t)\,dV_\chi\le C_T$.

For the spectral polynomial $G$, \cite[Proposition~4.16]{Linfty}
shows that $(G,\mathcal A)$ is an admissible pair satisfying the quasi-subharmonicity condition, and gives
\begin{equation}\label{increment}
 G(B+Q)-G(B)\ge a_d\binom nd\det\nolimits_\chi(Q)^{d/n}
 \qquad(B\in\mathcal A,\ Q\ge0).
\end{equation}
Apply this with $B=\underline A_t-\varrho I\in\mathcal A$. Both
$G(B)$ and $h_t^d$ are uniformly bounded, so
\[
 Q\ge0,\quad G(B+Q)\le h_t^d
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \det\nolimits_\chi Q\le C_T.
\]
Theorem~1.1 of \cite{Linfty} now applies with auxiliary form
$\varrho\chi$ and constant determinant density, proving the estimate.
head: environment

label: C2prop
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For \eqref{root-path}, Proposition~\ref{rootoperator} gives
concavity, ellipticity and
\[
 \operatorname{tr}\partial F(A)\ge\left(\binom nd a_d\right)^{1/d}>0.
\]
Moreover, $F$ vanishes on $\partial\mathcal C_G$, while $h_t\ge\delta_1^{1/d}$.
Proposition~\ref{raylemma} gives the subsolution bound
\eqref{quantitative-subsolution} and the alternatives
\eqref{alternatives}. Taking matrices diagonal in an eigenbasis of
$\underline A_t$ gives the eigenvalue subsolution condition used in
that proof. The bounds for $h_t$ and $\operatorname{osc}_Xv_t$ follow
from \eqref{rhs-bounds} and Proposition~\ref{C0prop}.

The domain $\mathcal C_G$ need not be a cone. In the second-order calculation,
the cone condition is used to control the negative eigenvalues by the
largest one. Here, if $\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n$ are the
eigenvalues of $A_t$, \eqref{tracebound} gives
\[
 \lambda_n\ge-C-(n-1)\lambda_1,\qquad
 |\lambda_i|\le C\lambda_1\quad\text{when }\lambda_1\ge1.
\]
This replaces the trace positivity in Sz\'ekelyhidi's calculation
of the largest eigenvalue; the resulting inequalities differ only
by fixed constants. His maximum-principle argument therefore yields
\[
 \sup_X\lambda_{\max}(A_t)
 \le C_T\bigl(1+\|\partial v_t\|_{L^\infty}^2\bigr).
\]
Using \eqref{tracebound} once more and subtracting
$\underline\omega_t$ proves \eqref{C2bound}.
head: environment

label: smoothprop
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{smoothprop}
For every finite $T$ and every integer $m\ge0$, the solutions of
\eqref{path} with $0\le t\le T$, normalized by either supremum zero
or integral zero, satisfy
\[
 \|v_t\|_{C^m}\le C_{m,T}.
\]
head: environment

label: limitPDE
title: Proof
body_md:
For the gradient bound, we use the standard blow-up argument of
Sz\'ekelyhidi \cite[Section~6]{Szekelyhidi}. If the bound fails, choose normalized
solutions $v_j$ and rescale at their gradient maximum points, in
holomorphic charts unitary at their centers:
\[
 r_j=\sup_X|\partial v_j|_\chi\longrightarrow\infty,
 \qquad w_j(z)=v_j(z/r_j).
\]
Propositions~\ref{C0prop} and~\ref{C2prop} give a subsequence with
\[
 w_j\longrightarrow w\text{ in }C^{1,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb C^n),
 \qquad |\partial w(0)|=1,
\]
where $w$ is bounded and globally Lipschitz. After rescaling, the
background and lower-degree terms vanish, leaving $a_d\sigma_d$.
The positive diagonal derivative inequalities on the admissible domain
select the $\Gamma_d$ branch and give
\begin{equation}\label{limitPDE}
 \lambda(dd^cw)\in\partial\Gamma_d,\qquad
 \Gamma_d=\{\sigma_1>0,\ldots,\sigma_d>0\},
\end{equation} in the viscosity sense.
For $d<n$, the Dinew--Ko{\l}odziej Liouville theorem
\cite[Theorem~0.1]{DK} makes $w$ constant. For $d=n$, bounded
plurisubharmonic functions on $\mathbb C^n$ are constant.
Both contradict $|\partial w(0)|=1$.

The gradient bound and \eqref{C2bound} give $\|A_t\|\le C_T$.
Since $G(A_t)\ge\delta_1$ and $G\le-\delta_1$ on
$\partial\mathcal A$, the solution matrices lie in
\[
 \{A\in\overline{\mathcal A}:\|A\|\le C_T,\ G(A)\ge\delta_1\}
 \Subset\mathcal C_G.
\]
Strict ellipticity of $F$ therefore gives uniform ellipticity near
all solution matrices. Using the complex Evans--Krylov theorem in \cite[Theorem~3.4 and Section~4]{TWWY},
we obtain a uniform $C^{2,\alpha}$ bound from \eqref{rhs-bounds}. Standard Schauder estimates give all higher bounds.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: In our previous joint work with Wu \cite{Liouville}, we obtained a full geometric characterization of Liouville rigidity for degenerate real and complex Hessian equations. In particular, the result applies to all spectral cases and provides an alternative to the Liouville theorem used above.
head: environment

label: startprop
title: Proposition
head: environment

label: Poissonlimit
title: Proof
body_md:
For $k\geq0,\alpha\in(0,1)$, let \[
 C^{k,\alpha}_0(X):=\left\{v\in C^{k,\alpha}(X,\mathbb R)\,|\ \int_XvdV_\chi=0\right\}.\]
Set $\tau=t^{-1}$. For $v\in C^{2,\alpha}_0(X)$, write $\underline{\omega}_v:=\underline \omega+dd^c v$ and define
\[
 \mathcal G(\tau,v)=\tau^{d-1}
 \bigl[P_x(\tau^{-1}I+A_{\underline{\omega}_v})-b(\tau^{-1})\bigr].
\]
Since $$\frac{(\Lambda\wedge e^{\underline{\omega}_v+t\chi})^{[n]}}{\chi^n/n!}= 
\binom nd a_{d}t^d+O(t^{d-1}),\qquad b(t)=\binom nd  a_dt^d+O(t^{d-1}),$$
the expansion 
shows that the leading $t^d$ terms in $P_x(tI+A_{\underline{\omega}_v})-b(t)$ cancel. Thus $\mathcal G$ extends smoothly to $\tau=0$, with
\begin{equation}\label{Poissonlimit}
 \mathcal G(0,v)=\binom{n-1}{d-1}a_d
 \left(\Delta_\chi v+\operatorname{tr}_\chi\underline\omega
       -\int_X\operatorname{tr}_\chi\underline\omega\,dV_\chi\right).
\end{equation}
The equation $\mathcal G(0,v)=0$ has a unique smooth
solution $v_*$ with zero average. For every $\tau$ and $v$, the map has integral zero:
\[
 \int_X\mathcal G(\tau,v)\,dV_\chi=0.
\]
At $(0,v_*)$, the derivative in $v$ is the isomorphism
\[
 \binom{n-1}{d-1}a_d\Delta_\chi:
 C^{2,\alpha}_0(X)\longrightarrow C^{0,\alpha}_0(X),
\]
where the subscript denotes integral zero. The implicit-function
theorem gives $v_\tau$ for small positive $\tau$, uniformly bounded in
$C^{2,\alpha}$. For $t=\tau^{-1}$ sufficiently large,
\[
 \omega_t=t\chi+\underline\omega+dd^cv_\tau>0.
\]
Its eigenvalues are $t+O(1)$ and therefore belong to $\mathcal A$. Elliptic regularity makes $\omega_t$ smooth.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume \textup{(i)}. Choose $T$ large enough for
Proposition~\ref{startprop}, and let $\mathcal S\subset[0,T]$ be the
set of parameters for which \eqref{path} has a smooth admissible
solution, normalized by integral zero. Then $T\in\mathcal S$.

For openness, the map
\[
 v\longmapsto P_x(A_{\underline\omega_t+dd^cv})-b(t)
\]
takes values in mean-zero functions by \eqref{bt}.
Its linearization at a solution is
\begin{equation}\label{linearization}
 L_tw\,\frac{\chi^n}{n!}=dd^cw\wedge\Xi_t,
 \qquad \Xi_t=(\Lambda\wedge e^{\omega_t})^{[n-1]}.
\end{equation}
The form $\Xi_t$ is closed and strictly positive, since $P_i>0$ on
$\mathcal A$. For real smooth $w,z$, integration by parts gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \int_XwL_tz\,\frac{\chi^n}{n!}
 &=-\operatorname{Re}\int_X\sqrt{-1}\,
         \partial w\wedge\bar\partial z\wedge\Xi_t\\
 &=\int_XzL_tw\,\frac{\chi^n}{n!}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The kernel consists of constants by ellipticity and the maximum
principle. Self-adjointness and Fredholm theory make $L_t$ an
isomorphism between the mean-zero H\"older spaces, so the
implicit-function theorem proves openness.

For closedness, Proposition~\ref{smoothprop} gives uniform bounds on
$[0,T]$ and keeps the solution matrices in a compact subset of
$\mathcal A$. If $t_j\in\mathcal S$ converges, a subsequence of the
normalized solutions converges smoothly. Its limit solves the
endpoint equation and remains admissible. Hence $\mathcal S$ is closed,
and connectedness gives $\mathcal S=[0,T]$.
At $t=0$, $b(0)=0$ and $[\omega_t]=[\omega_0]$, so $\omega_t$ satisfies \eqref{target}, proving \textup{(ii)}.

Conversely, a solution in \textup{(ii)} lies in
$\overline{\mathcal C_{P_x}}\subset\mathcal A$ by \eqref{admissible-levels}, and
therefore supplies \textup{(i)}.
For uniqueness, let $\omega_u,\omega_v$ be two solutions. Both belong
to $\mathcal C_G$ and satisfy $F(A_u)=F(A_v)=h_0(x)$. Concavity gives
\[
 0=F(A_u)-F(A_v)
 \le\partial F(A_v)[\chi^{-1}dd^c(u-v)].
\]
The right-hand side is a smooth strictly elliptic linear operator
applied to $u-v$. The maximum principle on the connected compact
manifold forces $u-v$ to be constant.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume \textup{(i)}. Replace $a_0(x)$ by its average
$\bar a_0=\int_Xa_0\,dV_\chi$ and put
$\bar P=\widetilde P+\bar a_0$. This preserves compatibility and the
mixed intersection classes of degree $q<n$. Moreover,
\[
 -\bar P(\rho_1\mathbf1)=-\int_XP_x(\rho_1 \mathbf1)\,dV_\chi>0,\qquad
 \int_X\bar P(A_{\omega_0})\,dV_\chi=0.
\]
Its diagonal restriction satisfies \eqref{strict}, and its first
derived component is $\mathcal A$. Write its monic diagonal restriction as
\[
 \frac{\bar P(s\mathbf1)}{\binom nd a_d}
 =s^d-\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}\binom di c_i s^i.
\]
For $m=d-n+q$, direct differentiation gives
\[
 \frac{n!\,\bigl(\Lambda\wedge e^\alpha\bigr)^{[q]}}{\binom nd a_d}
 =\frac{d!}{m!}[\chi]^{n-d}
 \left(\alpha^m-
 \sum_{i=0}^{m-1}\binom mi c_{n-q+i}\alpha^i[\chi]^{m-i}\right),
\]
with the sum empty when $m=0$. These are positive multiples of the
mixed classes in the numerical criterion of Fu--Li--Zhang--Zhang
\cite[Theorem~1.2]{FLZZ}. By assumption \textup{(i)}, that theorem
gives a smooth closed representative $\omega_\tau\in\alpha$ with
$A_{\omega_\tau}\in\mathcal C_{\bar P+\tau}$ for every sufficiently small
$\tau>0$. Choose $\tau<-\bar P(\rho_1\mathbf1)$. Then $\bar P+\tau$ still
satisfies \eqref{strict}, so
\[
 \mathcal C_{\bar P+\tau}
 \subset\bigcap_{i=1}^n\mathcal C_{\partial_i\bar P}
 =\mathcal A.
\]
This proves $\textup{(i)}\Longrightarrow\textup{(ii)}$.
Theorem~\ref{main} gives
$\textup{(ii)}\Longleftrightarrow\textup{(iii)}$ and uniqueness.

Finally, assume \textup{(ii)} and choose its admissible representative
$\underline\omega$. In a $\chi$-unitary coframe diagonalizing
$\underline\omega$, the coefficients of
$(\Lambda\wedge e^{\underline\omega})^{[q]}$, for $n-d\le q<n$, are
coordinate derivatives of $\widetilde P$ of order $n-q$. These are
nonzero since $a_d>0$, and positive on $\mathcal A$ by
Proposition~\ref{idealinputs}\textup{(i)}, applied to the first
derivatives of $\widetilde P$.
Compactness therefore gives a common $\delta_{\mathrm{num}}>0$ such that
\[
 (\Lambda\wedge e^{\underline\omega})^{[q]}-\delta_{\mathrm{num}}\chi^q
 \quad\text{is strongly positive}.
\]
For every K\"ahler class $\kappa$, wedging with the $(k-q)$th power of
a K\"ahler representative of $\kappa$ and integrating over $Y$ gives
\eqref{uniform-numerical}. In particular,
$\textup{(ii)}\Longrightarrow\textup{(i)}$.
head: environment

label: nhr:spectral-verification
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{nhr:spectral-verification}
Let $\omega$ be an admissible solution of the spectral equation in
Theorem~\ref{main}, with $\Lambda$ given by \eqref{Lambda-def}.
Then \ref{H1}--\ref{H2} hold.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\Lambda$ is given by \eqref{Lambda-def},
$\mathcal F(\eta)/(\chi^n/n!)=P_x(A_\eta)$.
Lemmas~\ref{shiftlemma} and \ref{nhr:scalarization} show that
$P_\varepsilon$ is ideal G\aa rding elliptic for all sufficiently small
$\varepsilon\ge0$. This gives \ref{H1}.
For $\varepsilon>0$, we have $A_\omega\in\mathcal A$ and
$\mathcal F_\varepsilon(\omega)>0$, so
\eqref{componentidentity} gives $A_\omega\in\mathcal C_{P_\varepsilon}$,
proving \ref{H0solution}.

Finally, $\Lambda^{[n-d]}=a_d\chi^{n-d}/(n-d)!$ is strictly positive,
and its terminal mixed pairings are nondegenerate by the mixed
Hodge--Riemann theorem \cite[Proposition~2.1]{NHRDN}. This gives
\ref{H2}.
head: environment

label: nhr:pointwise
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{nhr:pointwise}
Assume \ref{H1}--\ref{H2} and fix $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0$. Let
$B=(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_j)$ be a tuple of K\"ahler forms,
$0\le j\le d-2$, and put $m=d-j$. At each point of $X$, the polynomial
\[
 g=\frac{\partial^B\mathcal F_\varepsilon}{\chi^n/n!}
\]
is positive and strictly elliptic on a neighborhood of $\omega$ in the
space of real $(1,1)$-forms, and $g^{1/m}$ and $\log g$ are concave there.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix a point of $X$. By \ref{H1} and \ref{H0solution}, $P_{\varepsilon}$ is
ideal G\aa rding elliptic and $\omega\in\mathcal C_{P_{\varepsilon}}$.
The degree-$m$ homogeneous part of $g=\partial^B P_{\varepsilon}$,
evaluated at $\chi$, is
\[
 \frac{\beta_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\beta_j\wedge\chi^m
       \wedge\Lambda^{[n-d]}}{m!\,\chi^n/n!}>0
\]
by \ref{H2}. Thus $g$ has degree exactly $m$.
Lemma~\ref{ige:basic}\textup{(iii)} gives positivity of $g$ and
concavity of $g^{1/m}$ and $\log g$ on $\mathcal C_{P_{\varepsilon}}$,
which contains a neighborhood of $\omega$.

For a nonzero rank-one semipositive form $\eta$, the degree-$(m-1)$
homogeneous part of $\partial_\eta g$, evaluated at $\chi$, is
\[
 \frac{\beta_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\beta_j\wedge\eta\wedge\chi^{m-1}
       \wedge\Lambda^{[n-d]}}{(m-1)!\,\chi^n/n!}>0.
\]
Hence $\partial_\eta g$ is nonzero and positive on $\mathcal C_{P_{\varepsilon}}$
by the same lemma. This proves strict ellipticity.
head: environment

label: nhr:strict
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{nhr:strict}
Assume \ref{H1}--\ref{H2}. For every K\"ahler tuple $B$ of length
$0\le j\le d-2$, with $m=d-j$ and any
$0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0$, put
\[
 L_B=\partial(\partial^B\mathcal I)_\alpha,
 \qquad Q_B=\partial^2(\partial^B\mathcal I)_\alpha.
\]
Then $Q_B$ has signature $(1,h^{1,1}(X)-1)$ and is negative definite
  on $\ker L_B$. Moreover, for any $u\in H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)$, \begin{equation}\left(\int_X\partial^B\mathcal F_\varepsilon(\omega)\right)
 Q_B(u,u)\le\frac{m-1}{m}L_B(u)^2.\label{nhr:global-root}\end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose K\"ahler representatives of $B$, fix
$0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0$, and put $m=d-j$.
At each point, consider
\[
 g_k=\frac{\partial_\chi^k\partial^B\mathcal F_\varepsilon}
                {\chi^n/n!},\qquad 0\le k\le m-2.
\]
Lemma~\ref{nhr:pointwise} gives positivity and log concavity near
$\omega$ at every level. The Hessian of $g_{m-2}$ is a positive multiple of
\[
 (\eta,\zeta)\longmapsto
 \frac{\eta\zeta\beta_1\cdots\beta_j\chi^{m-2}\Lambda^{[n-d]}}
      {\chi^n/n!},
\]
which is nondegenerate by \ref{H2}.

All derivatives in the following pointwise argument are evaluated at
$\omega$. Suppose $\partial g_k[v]=\partial^2g_k[v,v]=0$.
Negative semidefiniteness of $\partial^2\log g_k$ implies
$\partial^2g_k[v,w]=0$ for every $w$, and hence
$\partial g_{k+1}[v]=0$ when $k<m-2$.
For $k<m-2$, the nonpositive function $\partial^2\log g_k[v,v]$
attains zero at $\omega$, so
\[
 0=\partial_\chi\bigl(\partial^2\log g_k[v,v]\bigr)
   =\frac{\partial^2g_{k+1}[v,v]}{g_k}.
\]
Iterating reaches the quadratic endpoint, where its nondegenerate
Hessian forces $v=0$. Thus $\partial^2g_0$ is strictly negative on
$\ker\partial g_0$.

For $u\in H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)$, take a closed representative $\eta$
and solve
\begin{equation}\label{nhr:corrector}
 \partial(\partial^B\mathcal F_\varepsilon)_\omega
       [\eta+dd^c\varphi]
 =\frac{L_B(u)}{\int_X\partial^B\mathcal F_\varepsilon(\omega)}
       \partial^B\mathcal F_\varepsilon(\omega).
\end{equation}
The first derivative is strictly elliptic, and its defining form is
closed. The operator in $\varphi$ is therefore self-adjoint with
kernel the constants. The equation has zero integral after subtracting
$\partial(\partial^B\mathcal F_\varepsilon)_\omega[\eta]$ from both
sides, so it has a smooth solution, unique modulo constants.


Apply the concavity of $g_0^{1/m}$ to $\eta_\varphi:=\eta+dd^c \varphi$ and use \eqref{nhr:corrector} to obtain \begin{align}   \partial^2g_0[\eta_\varphi,\eta_\varphi]&\leq\frac{m-1}{m}\frac{(\partial g_0[\eta_\varphi])^2}{g_0(\omega)}\\
    &=\frac{m-1}{m}\left(\frac{L_B(u)}{\int_X\partial^B\mathcal F_{\varepsilon}(\omega)}\right)^2\,g_0.\notag
\end{align}
The forms defining the second derivative of
$\partial^B\mathcal F_\varepsilon$ at $\omega$ are closed.  By Stokes'
theorem, integrating against $\chi^n/n!$ gives
\begin{equation}
 \left(\int_X\partial^B\mathcal F_\varepsilon(\omega)\right)
 Q_B(u,u)\le\frac{m-1}{m}L_B(u)^2.
\end{equation}

If $0\not=u\in\ker L_B$, $\eta_\varphi$ cannot vanish identically, so the strict pointwise
negativity gives $$Q_B(u,u)=\int_X \partial^2g_0(\omega)[\eta_\varphi,\eta_\varphi]\,\frac{\chi^n}{n!}<0.$$
Evaluating at $\chi$ gives $L_B([\chi])>0$ and
$Q_B([\chi],[\chi])>0$, proving the signature.
head: environment

label: nhr:master
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First suppose that $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0$ and the $\beta_i$
are K\"ahler. Choose K\"ahler representatives.
Put $f(\mathbf{x})=\mathcal I(\alpha+\sum_i x_i\beta_i)+\varepsilon$.
For a multi-index $\nu$ with $|\nu|=j\le d-2$, set
$g=\partial_{\mathbf{x}}^\nu f$, $m=d-j$, and
\[
 J=g(0),\qquad b=\nabla g(0),\qquad Q_\nu=\partial^2g(0).
\]
The polynomial $g$ is the integral of the corresponding mixed
derivative of $\mathcal F_\varepsilon$.
Inequality~\eqref{nhr:global-root} gives
\[
 J>0,\qquad Q_\nu-\frac{m-1}{mJ}bb^T\le0.
\]
The Hessian of
$\partial_y^{m-2}\partial_{\mathbf{x}}^\nu\mathcal T_{\alpha,\varepsilon}$ is
\[
 (m-2)!
 \begin{pmatrix}
  m(m-1)J &(m-1)b^T\\
  (m-1)b &Q_\nu
 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its Schur complement is negative semidefinite, so it has exactly
one positive eigenvalue. These are all coordinate derivatives of
order $d-2$.

At each point $p\in X$, put
$h_p(\mathbf{x})=P_{\varepsilon}(A_\omega(p)+\sum_i x_iB_i)$,
where $B_i=\chi^{-1}\beta_i>0$.
By \ref{H1} and \ref{H0solution}, $h_p$ is ideal G\aa rding with the origin in its component.
Every iterated coordinate derivative of order at most $d$ is nonzero
by \ref{H2} and positive at the origin by
Proposition~\ref{idealinputs}\textup{(i)}. Thus every degree-$d$ monomial in
$y^dh_p(\mathbf{x}/y)$ has a positive coefficient. Integration over $X$
preserves positivity, including the coefficient $\varepsilon$ of $y^d$.
The support is therefore the full simplex of degree-$d$ multi-indices.
The Hessian criterion of Br\"and\'en--Huh
\cite[Theorem~2.25]{NHRBH} now shows that
$\mathcal T_{\alpha,\varepsilon}$ is Lorentzian.

For nef classes $\beta_i$ and $0\le\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0$, take
$0<\tau<\varepsilon_0-\varepsilon$ and put
$\beta_i^{(\tau)}=\beta_i+\tau[\chi]$. These classes are K\"ahler, so the polynomials
\[
 y^d\left[\mathcal I\!\left(\alpha+
       \frac1y\sum_{i=1}^N x_i\beta_i^{(\tau)}\right)+\varepsilon+\tau\right]
\]
are Lorentzian by the preceding argument.
Since the Lorentzian class is closed
\cite[Theorem~2.25]{NHRBH}, taking $\tau\to0$ proves the assertion.
head: environment

label: nhr:lefschetz
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Theorem~\ref{nhr:strict} gives the signature, and Hodge--Poincar\'e duality
gives \eqref{nhr:cup-isomorphism}. On a projective $X$, the divisor
subspace contains an ample class of positive square, so the restriction
is nondegenerate. The perfect numerical pairing identifies
$N^1(X)_{\mathbb R}^{*}$ with $N_1(X)_{\mathbb R}$, giving
\eqref{nhr:numerical-lefschetz}.
head: environment

label: nhr:hodge-index
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{nhr:hodge-index}
Let $\mathcal D$ be the component of $\{\gamma\in H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R):Q(\gamma,\gamma)>0\}$
containing $[\chi]$. For
$\gamma,\eta\in\mathcal D$,
\begin{equation}\label{nhr:AF-inequality}
 \left(\int_X\gamma\eta\,\Theta\right)^2
 \ge\left(\int_X\gamma^2\Theta\right)
     \left(\int_X\eta^2\Theta\right),
\end{equation}
with equality exactly when $\gamma$ and $\eta$ are positively
proportional. The weak inequality extends to nef classes.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Mixed positivity places the K\"ahler cone in $\mathcal D$.
For $\gamma,\eta\in \mathcal D$, write $\eta=b\gamma+\eta_0$, where
$b>0$ and $Q(\gamma,\eta_0)=0$. The orthogonal complement of $\gamma$
is negative definite, so
\[
 Q(\gamma,\eta)^2-Q(\gamma,\gamma)Q(\eta,\eta)
 =-Q(\gamma,\gamma)Q(\eta_0,\eta_0)\ge0,
\]
with equality exactly when $\eta_0=0$. Approximation by K\"ahler classes
gives the weak inequality for nef classes.
head: environment

label: nhr:fivefold
title: Example
body_md:
\label{nhr:fivefold}
Let
\[
 X=\mathbb P^3\times\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^1,
 \qquad [\chi]=A+B+C,
 \qquad \alpha=3A-\frac18B+8C,
\]
where $A,B,C$ are the hyperplane pullbacks. Then
$A^4=B^2=C^2=0$ and $\int_XA^3BC=1$.
Take
\[
 \Lambda=\frac15\chi-\frac1{10}\chi^3
         +\frac7{120}\chi^4-\frac7{320}\chi^5.
\]
The diagonal restriction
\(
 p_x(s)=s^4-6s^2+7s-\frac{21}{8}
\)
has the monotone root sequence
\[
 \rho_0>\rho_1>\rho_2=1>\rho_3=0.
\]
The intersection ring gives $\mathcal I(\alpha)=0$ and, in cohomology,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \Lambda\wedge e^\alpha
 &=\frac15[\chi]+\frac{24A^2+23AB+88AC+63BC}{40}\\
 &\quad+\frac{32A^3+21A^2B+216A^2C+157ABC}{40}\\
 &\quad+\frac{16A^3B+796A^3C+363A^2BC}{120}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Each nonzero homogeneous component has a smooth strictly positive
representative, so
Corollary~\ref{cor:numerical-solvability} gives a smooth admissible
solution in the non-nef class $\alpha$.

Here
\[
 \Theta=\frac1{10}[\chi](\alpha^2-[\chi]^2).
\]
The pairing $\int_Xuv\Theta$ has signature $(1,2)$, and cup product
with $\Theta$ gives an isomorphism
$H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)\simeq H^{4,4}(X,\mathbb R)$.
This class is not a product of nef classes: expansion of such a
product shows that the product of its $A^2B$ and $A^2C$ coefficients
is at least the product of its $A^3$ and $ABC$ coefficients, whereas
\[
 \frac{21}{40}\frac{27}{5}-\frac45\frac{157}{40}
 =-\frac{61}{200}<0.
\]
Its signature also follows from Xiao's $4$-positive theorem
\cite[Theorem~A]{Xiao21a}.
head: environment
name: A non-nef solution class on a fivefold

label: nhr:quintic
title: Example
body_md:
\label{nhr:quintic}
Let
\[
 X=\mathbb P^3\times\mathbb P^2,
 \qquad [\chi]=A+B,\qquad \alpha=2A+B,
\]
where $A,B$ are the hyperplane pullbacks. Then $A^4=B^3=0$ and
$\int_XA^3B^2=1$. Take
\[
 \Lambda=1-\frac1{20}\chi^2-\frac1{60}\chi^3
          -\frac{17}{1200}\chi^5.
\]
The diagonal restriction
\[
 p_x(s)=s^5-s^3-s^2-\frac{17}{10}
\]
has the monotone root sequence
\[
 \rho_0>\rho_1=1>\rho_2>\rho_3=\frac1{\sqrt{10}}>\rho_4=0.
\]
The intersection ring gives $\mathcal I(\alpha)=0$ and, in cohomology,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \Lambda\wedge e^\alpha
 &=1+2A+B+\frac{39A^2+38AB+9B^2}{20}\\
 &\quad+\frac{73A^3+102A^2B+45AB^2}{60}
       +\frac{110A^3B+63A^2B^2}{120}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Each nonzero homogeneous component has a smooth strictly positive
representative, so Corollary~\ref{cor:numerical-solvability} gives a
smooth admissible solution in $\alpha$. This equation is also covered
by  \cite{FMForms}.

Since $[\chi]$ and $\alpha$ are ample, Theorem~\ref{nhr:master} shows that
\[
 \mathcal T_{\alpha,0}(y,\mathbf{x})
 =y^5\mathcal I\!\left(\alpha+
             \frac{x_1[\chi]+x_2\alpha}{y}\right)
\]
is Lorentzian. Direct calculation gives
\[
 \det\partial^2\mathcal T_{\alpha,0}(1,0,0)
 =\frac{64387}{6000}\ne0.
\]
Every polynomial $\int_X(yu+x_1v+x_2w)^5$, with
$u,v,w\in H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)$, factors through the two-dimensional
space $H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)$ and hence has a singular Hessian.
Thus $\mathcal T_{\alpha,0}$ cannot be a homogeneous volume polynomial
on this same $X$.
head: environment
name: A non-volume homogenization
